They may also be called "those liberated by time" (*samayavimukta*), because they attain liberation only when waiting for the proper time.
At that time, there are six kinds [of favorable conditions]:

first, obtaining fine clothing; second, obtaining fine food; third, obtaining fine bedding; fourth, obtaining a favorable location; fifth, obtaining a person who can explain the Dharma well; and sixth, obtaining good companions in study. Without these, one cannot attain liberation.

This refers to those in the stage of training who possess the lineage of faith-understanding (*śraddhādhimukta-gotra*); they likewise possess both wisdom-liberation (*prajñā-vimukti*) and liberation-through-both [wisdom and concentration], as explained previously.
Among those of sharp and dull faculties, the one liberated by wisdom (*prajñā-vimukta*) does not possess [the supernormal powers] such as the absence of conflict (*araṇā*) and so forth.

Therefore, what is called "wholesome" (kuśala) is a general designation for both; just as taming a wild horse, departing from all that is unwholesome, and casting off the heavy burden are all termed "wholesome."

Regarding the nine knowledges and ten knowledges, according to the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* and the Sarvāstivāda school, there is one conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), because it mostly takes conventional objects such as vases and the like as its cognitive domain.
Second is the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), which refers to that which takes the four noble truths of the desire realm as its object.
Third is subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), which takes the four noble truths of the two upper realms as its object.
Fourth is the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), which is the knowledge of the truth of suffering.
Fifth is the knowledge of origination, because it is the knowledge of the truth of origination.
Sixth is the knowledge of cessation, because it is the knowledge of the truth of cessation.
Seventh is the knowledge of the path, because it is the knowledge of the truth of the path.
Eighth is the knowledge of others' minds, because it takes the minds of others as its object.
Ninth is the knowledge of exhaustion, because it exhausts all that exists.
Tenth is the knowledge of non-arising, because it takes non-arising as its object.
Among these ten knowledges, the first is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*), while the remaining eight are uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Other mental knowledges may be either contaminated or uncontaminated.
As for the distinction regarding their objects: conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) universally takes all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena as its objects.
Dharma-knowledge takes the four truths of the desire realm as its object;
subsequent knowledge takes the four truths of the higher realms as its object;
and the knowledge of others' minds takes the minds of others as its object.

At the initial moment when the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows and the knowledge of non-arising arise, they take only the aggregates of the Peak of Existence as their objects, specifically those categorized as suffering and its origin; therefore, it is only at a later stage that they are able to universally take all four truths as their objects.

Regarding the distinction between these two: first, when a noble one who possesses the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) initially realizes the fruit of arhatship, if they correctly know for themselves and, arising from samādhi, speak these words:
"I have known suffering; I have abandoned the origin; I have realized cessation; I have cultivated the path."
This is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
As for the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), having realized it for themselves, the noble ones speak these words:
"I have already known suffering; there is nothing further to be known."
I have already abandoned the origin; it need not be abandoned again.
I have already realized cessation; it need not be realized again.
I have already cultivated the path; it need not be cultivated again.
This is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). According to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*,

the Sautrāntika school maintains that knowing present phenomena is called "knowledge of phenomena" (*dharma-jñāna*), while knowing past and future phenomena is termed "subsequent knowledge" (*anvaya-jñāna*).
The remaining knowledges are as described above.
An Arhat of dull faculties possesses the first nine knowledges; they may give rise to afflictions and thus regress from the blissful abiding in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).

An Arhat of sharp faculties, however, possesses all ten knowledges; after attaining the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), they no longer give rise to afflictions and do not regress from the blissful abiding in the present life.
The second fascicle of the *Xianyang* (*Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*) also elucidates the ten knowledges; this has already been recounted by those who delight in such matters.

As for "having accomplished what was to be done," this is identical to the expression found in various sūtras: "that which was to be done has been done" and "that which was to be accomplished has been accomplished."
This means that all those beyond training (aśaikṣas) have attained superior remedies capable of severing the enemies of afflictions and birth-and-death.

The fruit of the maturation of karma is precisely the Truth of Suffering; the causes of karma and afflictions are precisely the Truth of Origination. By knowing suffering and abandoning origination, one brings an end to the stream of birth-and-death; this realization is called "having performed what was to be done" (*kṛtakṛtya*).
The liberation realized is precisely the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*), and the sublime wisdom that realizes it is precisely the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
Since all meritorious qualities such as the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) have been cultivated without exception, this is called "having accomplished what was to be accomplished."
Having already abandoned the heavy obstacles and having already perfected supreme virtues, they are therefore called "those who have done what was to be done.
From this third point, the differences in contemplation are distinguished.
What is their meaning?
Sūtra: The three contemplations on the provisional and the real, and the three contemplations on the gates of emptiness.
Explanation:
This clarifies the two gates of contemplation to manifest the practice of antidotes.

Regarding the third, the contemplation of the conventional and the real, there are the contemplations of the conventionality and reality of phenomena (*dharma*), of sensation (*vedanā*), and of names (*nāman*), as found in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and in the following text.
"Dharmas" refers to the phenomena of the five aggregates, consisting of both form and mind.
They are called "dharmas" because they maintain their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and serve as a basis for generating conceptual understanding.

Arising from a multitude of conditions, like illusory persons and the like, they lack reality in terms of being either self-dependent or other-dependent; therefore, they are said to be "provisional" (*prajñapti*).
Characteristics lack intrinsic nature; their essence is solely suchness (*tathatā*). Since suchness is immutable, it is described as "real.
Contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) refers to the mind capable of illumination through right wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*).
From this perspective, the single character "dharma" designates the object of contemplation.

The two terms "provisional" (*jia*) and "real" (*shi*) precisely define the characteristics of the practice: "provisional" refers to the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), and "real" refers to the ultimate (*paramārtha*).
The single term "contemplation" (*guan*) naturally illuminates the mind.

Regarding objects, there are general and specific categories; within the specific, there are the true and the conventional. Regarding wisdom, there are the preparatory (*prayoga*) and the fundamental (*mūla*). When both subject and object are manifested together, it is called the "contemplation of the provisional and real aspects of phenomena" (*dharmaprajñapti-vastu-guan*).

Regarding the contemplation of the provisional and the real nature of sensation (*vedanā*): among the universal mental factors, sensation is the intrinsic nature of feeling; it is the concomitance with all minds and mental states that experience; it is the objects of experience, such as suffering and pleasure; it is the karma experienced as merit or non-merit; and it is the fruit experienced as the maturation (*vipāka*) in the various realms of existence.

Because attachment to the flavors of birth and death is driven solely by the power of sensation (*vedanā*), it is established as a separate aggregate (*skandha*) among the mental factors (*caitasika*).
Since this fault is so grave, it is countered separately.
Whether they are nominal or substantial, and the nature of their contemplation, are as explained previously.

Regarding the contemplation of the nominal and the real: "name" refers to the designation used to express and define all phenomena, for it apprehends the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of phenomena rather than their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is essentially beyond names and speech; yet sentient beings, through deluded inversion, give rise to arbitrary attachments, conceiving of meanings based on names and conceiving of names based on meanings. Because of the power of false habitual tendencies accumulated since beginningless time, one correctly contemplates in order to eliminate these [attachments]. Other aspects of the nominal and the real are all as explained previously.
This pertains exclusively to the Mahāyāna; how could those beyond training (aśaikṣa) possess it? As previously cited, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The śrāvakas who are emanations (nirmāṇa) are in reality bodhisattvas; what fault is there in possessing this?"

Regarding the contemplation of the three gates of emptiness, these are the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta*), and the contemplation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
According to the *Abhidharmakośa*: "Among the four aspects of the Noble Truth of Suffering, one takes emptiness and selflessness as the gate of emptiness;

the four aspects of Cessation as the gate of signlessness; and the four aspects of each of Origination and the Path, along with the two aspects of suffering and impermanence—these ten aspects constitute the gate of wishlessness."

Question: Regarding the six aspects of the origin of suffering (*duḥkhasamudaya*), one is disenchanted with them because they are with outflows (*sāsrava*); since the path (*mārga*) is without outflows (*anāsrava*), why does the noble one not aspire to it? Answer:

While the Noble Path is not yet perfected, one constantly gives rise to aspirations and seeks; once the fruit of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) is complete, one no longer aspires to it. It is a necessary principle that one abandons the raft upon reaching the shore, for one has already transcended the objects currently present before them.

According to the first fascicle of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*: "The imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is empty of both self and phenomena; meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that takes this as its object is called the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*)."

Nirvāṇa is signless (*animitta*), for it is free from the ten signs; because one takes this as the object of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is called the door of liberation of the signless (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*).
As for the "ten signs," they are: the signs of form, sound, odor, taste, and touch; the signs of male and female; and the signs of birth, aging, and death—these constitute the ten signs.

"Contemplating the suffering of the three realms and having no aspirations or seeking—contemplating these through meditative concentration (samādhi)—is called the gate of liberation of wishlessness (apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha).
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it says: "To know the true reality (dharmatā) of phenomena as ultimate emptiness is called the samādhi of emptiness (śūnyatā-samādhi)."
To know that the true mark of all phenomena is signless, neither grasped nor attached to—this is called the samādhi of signlessness (*animitta-samādhi*).
Having known the emptiness of phenomena, not to contemplate whether phenomena are empty or not empty, or existent or non-existent—this is called the samādhi of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-samādhi*).
Regarding these three passages from the treatises: the first pertains exclusively to the Hīnayāna, while the latter two pertain exclusively to the Mahāyāna.
One should understand that the Arhat’s possession or lack thereof of both provisional and ultimate [attainments] is thus established.
The above three passages conclude the praise of his virtues; from here, the third section concludes with a summary praise of his accomplishments.
What is the meaning of this?
The Sūtra states:
"One fully accomplishes both conditioned merits and unconditioned merits."
The commentary states:
This praises the fact that all meritorious qualities are fully accomplished.

As for conditioned meritorious qualities, these include the factors of enlightenment within the body of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the knowledge of non-contention (*araṇā-jñāna*) and the knowledge resulting from vows (*praṇidhi-jñāna*), all untainted paths (*anāsrava-mārga*), tainted pure concentrations (*sāsrava-śuddha-samādhi*), the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*), the ten knowledges (*daśa-jñāna*) and their associated concentrations, and all such dharmas of merit.
The various concentrations (samādhi) are precisely the universal ground concentrations;
the various knowledges (jñāna) are precisely the universal ground wisdoms, which are conditioned virtues.
As for unconditioned merit, it refers to the virtue of unconditioned analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) present within the body of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).

According to the Sarvāstivāda school, there are eight patiences (*kṣānti*) within the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) for those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). In the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), there are nine grades for each of the nine stages. When the paths of seeing and cultivation are combined, there are eighty-nine grades in total.

The conditioned virtues, such as the paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and the unconditioned virtue of cessation through discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) realized by the eighty-nine grades of paths of liberation—these are called the unconditioned virtues of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
One should know that these two virtues of those in training (śaikṣa) are exclusively these.

However, according to the Mahāyāna school, they are provisionally established upon suchness (tathatā). Neither analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) nor non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) possesses a distinct substantial entity, nor do they have such categories or numerical distinctions. Rather, when the suchness (tathatā) is revealed in its perfection according to reality through wisdom (prajñā) being freed from obstructions, this is precisely what constitutes conditioned and unconditioned merits (guṇa).
Because she is endowed with the virtues of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), she is said to be "accomplished.
From this, secondly, [it concerns] the conclusion of the assembly of all nuns.
What is the meaning of this?
Sūtra: Furthermore, there was an assembly of eight hundred bhikṣuṇīs, all of whom were arhats.
Explanation:
This passage clarifies the community of *aśaikṣa* bhikṣuṇīs.
Within the text there are three parts:
"the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs" indicates the category and enumerates the group.
The term "bhikṣu" is as explained above; "ni" is a feminine suffix, for in the Sanskrit language there is this feminine form used to address her.
The phrase "eight hundred people together" indicates the number of the assembly.
"All are Arhats" means that all are praised as those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), for the meaning is as explained previously.
From this point, the third section concerns the inconceivable assembly of the hidden and the manifest.
This text is divided into three parts.
First, the enumeration and classification; second, the praise of virtues both collectively and individually; third, the concluding praise of accomplishment.
Regarding the first of these, the enumeration and classification: what is its meaning?
Sūtra: "Furthermore, there were immeasurable and incalculable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Explanation:
This indicates the assembly of bodhisattvas.

Regarding the terms "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) and "innumerable" (*asaṃkhyeya*), according to the forty-fifth chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, up to the one hundred and fourth [category] they are called "innumerable," and up to the one hundred and sixth they are called "immeasurable."
Although the order in which they are listed here in this sutra is not sequential, it clarifies that the assembly is vast; therefore, it is designated as "immeasurable and incalculable.

Furthermore, while the old sutra speaks of nine hundred million billion, this version merely says "immeasurable and incalculable" to signify their great number—why must it necessarily be that specific figure?
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva— Sanskrit for *bodhisattva*, here abbreviated as "Bodhisattva"—
the Sanskrit term *bodhi* is translated as "awakening."
In Sanskrit it is called *sattva*, which here means "sentient being.
Generally speaking, there are two gateways to the practice of a bodhisattva:
the first is self-benefit, for which great wisdom is primary;
The second is benefiting others, with great compassion as the foremost.
*Bodhi* means awakening; it is the fruit sought by wisdom.
*Sattva* refers to sentient beings; they are the living beings to be delivered through compassion.
Therefore, in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*,
Vasubandhu explains that one is called a "bodhisattva" based on the four great vows;
since both [the vows and the aspiration] belong to the objective sphere (*ālambana*), the term "bodhisattva" is a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*).
Furthermore, "awakening" (*bodhi*) refers to the fruit sought; "sentient being" (*sattva*) refers to the seeker of that fruit. A sentient being who seeks *bodhi* is called a *bodhisattva*.

Moreover, *bodhi* is precisely that which is sought; "sattva" here means "valiant. One who seeks great *bodhi* without shrinking from time or place, possessing both the will and the capability, is therefore named a *bodhisattva*.
These latter two interpretations both rely on the explanation provided by Bandhuprabha in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*, and both are *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compounds.

Furthermore, "bodhi" is itself "prajñā," while the term "sattva" is also called "upāya. Because these two dharmas are able to benefit and bring happiness to all sentient beings, the conventional designator is named "Bodhisattva. Thus, it is both "bodhi" and "sattva," and both are *karmadhāraya* (appositional determinative) compounds.
This is explained in detail in the *Amoghapāśa Sūtra*.
In Sanskrit it is called *mahā*, which here is translated as "Great.
*Sat* refers to *sattva*, the meaning of which has been explained previously.
As stated in the second fascicle of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*: "A Bodhisattva-mahāsattva refers to those sentient beings (*sattva*) who seek enlightenment (*bodhi*).
This term applies generally to all three vehicles; however, to distinguish them from those of the two [inferior] vehicles, the word "Great" (*mahā*) is added, such that they are all Mahāsattvas.
From this point, the second section provides a general and specific praise of virtues.
The text is divided into two parts:
first, the general praise of virtues; second, the specific praise of virtues.
First is the general praise of his virtues.
What is its meaning?
The Sūtra says:
"True wisdom is equanimous and eternally severs the obstacles of affliction; through skillful means, it gives rise to great practices and vows.
Explanation: This is a general praise of the two types of wisdom.
The first two lines clarify the wisdom of self-benefit, while the latter two lines clarify the wisdom of benefiting others.
However, each of these two types of wisdom has two names, as should be understood from the text itself.
What is called "wisdom of reality" (shijì zhì) is fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna).
"Reality" refers to the essence of True Suchness (tathatā), which is immutable; the wisdom that realizes this is termed "wisdom of reality.
What is called "equality" is because there is no distinction between high and low.
Regarding "the permanent severance of the obstacles of affliction": "affliction" refers to the *kleśas* (defilements), and "obstacles" refers to the two obstacles (*āvaraṇas*).

Those arising from conceptual discrimination are permanently severed at the first stage (*bhūmi*) through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*). As for the innate (*sahaja*) two obstacles, they are partially eliminated throughout the ten stages and only permanently severed upon reaching the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*); thus, the term "permanent severance" is used with respect to the first two obstacles, whereas the latter two obstacles are only exhausted upon reaching the final fruition (*phala*).

What is called "skillful means" (upāya) is subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna). Although it realizes that the dependent nature is like an illusion or a mirage, it does not abandon sentient beings through the extraction of their suffering by great compassion; this various benefiting of others is termed skillful means.
"Skillfulness in speech" means that the objects of conversion are skillfully matched to the suitability of their faculties, while the mind of the converter is skillfully able to remain non-abiding.
"Arousing great practices and vows" refers to initiating vast and sublime practices and vows.

This means that for Bodhisattvas prior to the seventh stage, conventional and ultimate wisdoms do not arise simultaneously; thus, whether their practices and vows are in a state of meditative concentration or distraction, they predominantly engage in post-meditative cultivation through effortful application.

Although from the eighth stage onward both the ultimate and conventional truths are taken as objects and practice proceeds spontaneously without requiring effort, in terms of their functional category, these are still considered "subsequently attained" wisdom.
Therefore, this passage speaks generally of the arousal of practices and vows.

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that both the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) are termed "actual wisdom" (*bhūtajñāna*), because they are able to take the two actual objects— ultimate truth and conventional truth— as their cognitive domains.
Their preparatory wisdom (*prayoga-jñāna*) is termed "expedient means" (*upāya*), because it is able to induce the arising of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment.
Although this interpretation does not contradict the meaning, we shall now adopt the former explanation.
Second, regarding the specific praise of his virtues: as the ten stages (*bhūmi*) differ, the text is divided into ten sections.
Now, concerning the characteristics of the first stage, what is its meaning?
Sūtra: One benefits sentient beings by means of the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*). Commentary:
This praises the practice of non-attachment.

When a bodhisattva brings relief to sentient beings, they attain compassion that identifies with them; at the very moment of truly benefiting others, it becomes self-benefit, for they do not perceive any benefit for others as being separate from themselves.
The four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) are for the purpose of gathering sentient beings.
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: "First is generosity (*dāna*): by means of material things such as food and clothing, one gathers in sentient beings."
Second is kind speech (*priyavāditā*), which involves speaking words that accord with another's inclinations in order to win their favor.
Third is beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*), which consists of seeking benefit for others and assisting them in accomplishing their affairs.
Fourth is cooperation (*samānārthatā*), such as when those on the same boat share the same joys and sorrows.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "To gather in sentient beings through the two kinds of wealth and Dharma is called giving (*dāna*).
To preach the six *pāramitās* for the sake of sentient beings is called kind speech (*priyavāditā*)."
To teach and transform sentient beings so that they practice the six perfections is called "beneficial conduct" (artha-caryā).

To employ various supernatural transformations through the power of spiritual penetrations (abhijñā) to enter the five destinies and engage in the same activities as all sentient beings is called "common purpose" (samānārthatā).
What are the functional activities of these four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*)?
As the eighth verse of the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* states: "They cause [beings] to become vessels, to gain faith, to practice, and also to understand."
"Performing these four deeds in sequence constitutes the activity of the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*).
According to the prose commentary, generosity enables one to become a vessel for the Dharma, because by being compliant with it, one becomes capable of receiving the Dharma."
Kind speech can cause one to give rise to faith in the Dharma, because through the teaching of its meaning, one's doubts are severed.
Beneficial conduct can cause one to give rise to practice regarding the Dharma, because one is able to act in accordance with the Dharma as it is taught.
Cooperative conduct (*samānārthatā*) enables others to attain liberation, because it brings about benefit through long-term practice.

In reality, all ten thousand practices are cultivated on the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*); however, this [stage] is praised specifically for its conformity with the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
What is the meaning of the second stage?
The Sūtra states:
"The four immeasurable minds universally cover all."
The commentary states:
This praises the practice of non-anger.
The Bodhisattva benefits sentient beings with impartiality toward both enemies and kin, acting as an uninvited friend who universally covers all.
The four immeasurables are loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Regarding the term "immeasurable," the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 81, states: "These four kinds are the sphere of extensive play for all the noble ones (*ārya*)."

Furthermore, these four take immeasurable sentient beings as their objects; because they produce immeasurable merit and lead to immeasurable results, they are called "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*). The *Xianyang lun* states:

"Because they are vast, because they are great, and because they are immeasurable—taking as their objects the entirety of the external container world and the world of sentient beings from one direction up to the ten directions, which are immeasurable and boundless—they are therefore called 'immeasurable'."

Regarding the meanings of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the others, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "Loving-kindness is defined as bestowing happiness; compassion (*karuṇā*) is defined as extracting from suffering; sympathetic joy (*muditā*) is defined as rejoicing; and equanimity (*upekṣā*) is defined as impartiality."

Furthermore, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: "Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is defined as a wholesome mind that is the opposite of hatred; compassion (*karuṇā*) is defined as a wholesome mind that is the opposite of malice; sympathetic joy (*muditā*) is defined as a wholesome mind that is the opposite of envy."
"These three are all distinctions of the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*); because they cause these three to be equal, it is called equanimity (*upekṣā*).

Furthermore, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states: "The immeasurable of loving-kindness is the desire to bestow the requisites of happiness upon those sentient beings who possess neither suffering nor pleasure."
Immeasurable compassion (*karuṇā*) is the desire to extract suffering from sentient beings who are in pain.
Immeasurable sympathetic joy (*muditā*) is to rejoice in the happiness of sentient beings who possess it.
Immeasurable equanimity (*upekṣā*) refers to a mind associated with equanimity that is free from attachment to its own mental disposition.

Regarding the determination of their essential nature, as stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, there are two views concerning the two types, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and compassion (*karuṇā*).
One view asserts that both have non-hatred (*adveṣa*) as their essential nature.
Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) serves as the antidote to anger that results in the taking of life; compassion (*karuṇā*) is said to be the antidote to anger that results in physical assault. Some say:
loving-kindness has non-anger (*adveṣa*) as its essence, while compassion has the root of goodness of non-harming (*avihiṃsā-kuśalamūla*) as its essence, because it counteracts the intent to harm.
Regarding joy (*prīti*), there are also two explanations.
Some say that its essence consists of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
Some say: Joy has exhilaration as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Equanimity has the wholesome root of non-attachment (*alobha*) as its essence; its associated mental factors and accompanying attendants are all of the nature of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Furthermore, according to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, these four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are all of the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*).

According to the Mahāyāna *Abhidharma-samuccaya-vyākhyā*, all four take both the two factors of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), as well as the various mental states and mental factors associated with them, as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Furthermore, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states: "Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) has non-hatred (*avyāpāda*) as its essential nature; compassion (*karuṇā*) has non-harming (*avihiṃsā*) as its essential nature; sympathetic joy (*muditā*) has non-envy (*anīrṣyā*) as its essential nature; and equanimity (*upekṣā*) has both non-greed (*alobha*) and non-hatred as its essential nature. All of these are dharmas characterized by pity for sentient beings."

Loving-kindness consists solely of non-hatred; compassion and sympathetic joy consist of a portion of non-hatred; and equanimity consists of a portion of both non-attachment and non-hatred, together with their associated mental factors as its essence.
In the Hīnayāna, these four are merely gates of contemplation; for the Bodhisattva who benefits others, all four are actual practices.
Next, regarding the meaning of the third stage (*bhūmi*), the Sūtra says:
The three types of clear knowledge are penetratingly realized, and the five supernormal powers are attained.
The commentary states:
this praises the possession of virtuous conduct.
In this stage, the Bodhisattva correctly eliminates ignorance, as they possess the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) associated with superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Regarding the "three types of clear knowledge" (*vidyā*) that provide penetrating insight, the older tradition states:

first, the clear knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-vidyā*); second, the clear knowledge of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-vidyā*); and third, the clear knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-vidyā*).

According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 101, it says: "First is the clear realization of the knowledge of recollecting past abodes, because it thoroughly penetrates and understands the phenomena of the prior limit.
Second is the clear realization of the knowledge of death and rebirth, because it thoroughly penetrates and understands the phenomena of the subsequent limit."
"The third is the realization of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānasākṣātkriyāvidyā*), because it penetrates and fully understands the nature of nirvāṇa.
The essence that reflects is wisdom (*prajñā*); the eye is able to illuminate the mind.
"Penetration" (*prativedha*) refers to thorough understanding; this is the object of observation.
Because they remedy ignorance regarding the three time periods, they are called "penetrating insights" (*vidyā*).

According to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, the essential nature of these three insights is as follows: the first two are of the nature of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) and are contaminated (*sāsrava*);
the latter is common to both contaminated and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), being of the nature of six or ten knowledges.

According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, all three are untainted (*anāsrava*); the former two are subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), and the latter is fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

Regarding those who attain the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), according to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, they are called "supernormal powers" because they involve an unerring and thorough comprehension of their respective objects, with wondrous functions that are unhindered and free from obstruction.

First is the supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of the divine realm (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna-sākṣātkriyā-abhijñā*). "Divine" (*ṛddhi*) refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*); "realm" (*vidhi*) refers to the performance of transformations; the unimpeded knowledge that realizes this divine realm is called "supernormal power" (*abhijñā*).

Second is the supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus-jñāna-sākṣātkriyā-abhijñā*). It is called "divine" because it is preeminent; it refers to the pure material faculty of the eye (*rūpa-dhātu-mahābhūta-śuddha-rūpa-cakṣur-indriya*) produced by the great elements of the form realm. "Knowledge" is the wisdom associated with visual consciousness; seeing at a distance without obstruction is called the "supernormal power of the divine eye."

The third is the supernormal power of the realization of the divine ear-wisdom (*divya-śrotra-jñāna-abhijñā*). It consists of the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) which is a pure form derived from the great elements of the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) associated with the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*). Because it hears at a distance without obstruction, it is called the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra-abhijñā*).
The fourth is the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (*paracitta-jñāna-abhijñā*). It is called "knowledge of others' minds" because it knows the minds of others.
From the perspective of the fundamental [attainment], one knows that what is known is not the mind, and that what is known as the mind is not [the actual] mind;
however, from the perspective of the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), it is termed the "supernormal power of others' minds."
The fifth is the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the recollection of past abodes; it consists of recollecting past events according to one's memory.

That is to say, by recollecting previous thoughts and observing them in reverse order, one is able to recollect even the initial moment of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*); this is called the fulfillment of the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
When the fundamental [attainment] is accomplished, one is able to recollect various past deeds—such as the specific places, surnames, and types of bodies—in which one existed;

this is called "recollection of former abodes" (*pūrvanivāsa*). This means that although that concentrated mind comprises many factors, the power of mindfulness is predominant; because wisdom follows the power of mindfulness to know those [past states], it is termed "following mindfulness" (*anusmṛti*).
The wisdom that realizes past lives without obstruction is called *abhijñā* (supernormal knowledge).

Regarding the five bodies [of these powers], according to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, these five *abhijñās* are subsumed within the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) constitutes their essential nature.

The supernormal powers of the divine realm (*ṛddhi-vidhi*), the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*), the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*), and the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsa-anusmṛti*)—these four all consist of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) and are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*).

The supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (*paracitta-jñāna-abhijñā*) has five knowledges as its essence: namely, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), and worldly knowledge (*loka-jñāna*); this is because the power of knowing others' minds takes both contaminated and uncontaminated states as its essence.
Regarding the basis (*āśraya-bhūmi*): in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the increase of cessation (*nirodha*) and tranquility (*śamatha*) is observed.

The five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) must necessarily rely on a level where both insight (*vipaśyanā*) and tranquility (*śamatha*) are balanced; according to the four fundamental dhyānas, they do not exist in the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*).

According to the *Xianyang lun* (Śāsanodbhāvana-śāstra), the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) all take the two dharmas of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), along with their associated factors, as their essence; they are subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) and are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).

It was previously stated that the three knowledges (*tisro vidyāḥ*) are themselves the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). Why, then, are they missing from within the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*)? Answer:

The three types of higher knowledge (*vidyā*) are explained here by way of defining them according to their own respective stages; however, when discussed generally across subsequent stages, they include all untainted (*anāsrava*) states.
Next, regarding the fourth stage, what is its meaning?
The Sūtra says:
"Cultivating the boundless factors of enlightenment" (bodhipakṣadharma) is explained as praising the practice of cultivation.
Regarding the term "boundless," it refers to the fact that through cultivation and repeated practice, [the qualities] become vast and limitless.
As for the "factors of enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣadharma*): *bodhi* means awakening, which is precisely that which is sought.
*Pakṣa* means cause, and also carries the sense of constituent parts.
The thirty-seven factors are conducive to awakening; because they are parts of awakening, they are called "factors of awakening" (*bodhipakṣa*).

Regarding the number thirty-seven, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "In this stage, the bodhisattva contemplates the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena internally and externally, applying diligent mindfulness and clear comprehension to eliminate worldly craving and attachment;

furthermore, he practices to diligently abandon unwholesome states that have not yet arisen or have already arisen, and to diligently increase wholesome states that have not yet arisen or have already arisen."
Furthermore, one cultivates the bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) through the perfection of desire, effort, mind, and investigation;

furthermore, one cultivates the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom, as well as the power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom;

furthermore, one cultivates the awakening factor of mindfulness, the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena, the awakening factor of energy, the awakening factor of joy, the awakening factor of tranquility, the awakening factor of concentration, and the awakening factor of equanimity.
Furthermore, one practices right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
Thus, there are thirty-seven [factors].

Regarding the substance (*dravya*) from which these emerge, the twenty-fifth verse of the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "In reality, these consist of only ten," namely: wisdom (*prajñā*), diligence (*vīrya*), concentration (*samādhi*), faith (*śraddhā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), joy (*prīti*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), as well as ethical discipline (*śīla*) and applied thought (*vitarka*). These constitute their essential nature.

Furthermore, wisdom (*prajñā*) comprises eight factors: namely, the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), the power of wisdom (*prajñābala*), the factor of awakening of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicayasaṃbodhyaṅga*), and right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*);

these have wisdom as their essence. Diligence (*vīrya*) also comprises eight factors: namely, the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*), the power of diligence (*vīryabala*), the factor of awakening of diligence (*vīryasaṃbodhyaṅga*), and right effort (*samyagvyāyāma*); these have diligence as their essence.

Concentration (*samādhi*) also comprises eight factors: namely, the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), the faculty of concentration, the power of concentration, the factor of enlightenment of concentration, and right concentration;
these have concentration as their essential nature. Faith (*śraddhā*) comprises only two: namely, the faculty of faith and the power of faith; these have faith as their essential nature.

Mindfulness comprises only four factors: namely, the faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, the awakening factor of mindfulness, and right mindfulness; these have mindfulness as their essential nature.
Joy comprises only one factor: namely, the awakening factor of joy; this has joy as its essential nature.

Equanimity (*upekṣā*) subsumes only one factor, namely the awakening-factor of equanimity; its essence is the equanimity of mental formations (*saṃskāra-upekṣā*), not the equanimity of feeling (*vedanā-upekṣā*).
Serenity (*praśrabdhi*) subsumes one factor, namely the awakening-factor of serenity; its essence is serenity itself.
Morality comprises only three factors—namely right speech, right action, and right livelihood—taking morality as their essence.
Applied thought comprises only one factor—namely right intention—taking applied thought as its essence.
Therefore, although there are thirty-seven [factors], their substance consists of only ten.

For those who practice these contemplations for the dual benefit of self and others, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "All are for the sake of not abandoning any sentient being, up to and including abiding in the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*)."
